books.title: Atomic Habits
books.author: James Clear
books.blurb: Tiny changes, remarkable results: how habits form, how identity drives them, and how to build good ones and break bad ones.

lessons.b: Small improvements compound into large results.
Lasting habits come from changing who you are, not chasing outcomes.
How habits form, and how to build them.

lessons.t: You can’t change what you can’t see
lessons.b: Before you change a habit, you have to notice it.

lessons.t: The best way to start a new habit
lessons.b: Give every habit a time and a place.
Change what you see, and you change what you do.
The most self-controlled people are the least tempted.

lessons.t: How to make a habit irresistible
lessons.b: The second law: make it attractive.

lessons.t: How family and friends shape your habits
lessons.b: We copy the habits of the people around us.

books.title: Rich Dad Poor Dad
books.author: Robert T. Kiyosaki (with Sharon Lechter)

lessons.t: The Rich Don't Work for Money
lessons.b: Through young Robert's low-paid job at rich dad's store, the book shows how fear and desire keep people chasing paychecks, and why learning to make money work for you is the way out of the rat race.
Wealth comes from building a column of assets that put money in your pocket, like businesses and rental property, rather than buying liabilities, including a home you live in, which take money out.

Your profession is not your business, so keep your day job while steadily building your own column of assets, much as McDonald's grew rich from the land under its restaurants and not only from selling burgers.

lessons.t: Taxes and the Power of Corporations
lessons.b: Understanding tax law and using corporations lets the rich earn, spend, and then pay tax on what remains, while employees are taxed before they ever see their pay.
Financial knowledge lets you see deals others miss and create your own luck, such as buying property cheaply when a market crashes and everyone else is afraid.

lessons.t: Work to Learn, Not to Earn
lessons.b: Choose jobs for the skills they teach, especially selling, communication and managing systems, because many people can cook a better burger than McDonald's but few can build the business behind it.
Cynicism, laziness, bad habits and arrogance hold people back, and simple shifts like paying yourself first and asking how you can afford something help you break through them.
Turning these lessons into wealth starts with a strong personal reason, a daily choice to spend time and money on learning and assets, and small first steps taken now.

books.blurb: Robert Kiyosaki tells the story of growing up in Hawaii with two father figures. His own father was highly educated and held a respected government job, yet he struggled with money all his life. His best friend's father left school early but built real wealth through businesses and property. Through the lessons of this rich dad, Kiyosaki argues that schools teach people to work for money but rarely teach how money actually works. He urges readers to learn the difference between assets, which put money in your pocket, and liabilities, which take money out. He warns that fear and desire keep people trapped in a cycle of earning and spending that he calls the rat race. His answer is financial literacy, steadily building assets, and choosing work for what it teaches rather than just the paycheck.

books.title: Never Split the Difference
books.author: Chris Voss with Tahl Raz

lessons.b: People decide with their emotions first, so winning a negotiation starts with understanding feelings rather than out-arguing someone with logic.
Repeating the last few words someone said, in a calm and slow voice, makes them feel heard and gets them to reveal more.
Labeling the other person's emotions, and even listing their likely complaints about you up front, defuses fear and builds trust.

lessons.t: Aim for No, Then That's Right
lessons.b: Letting people say no makes them feel safe and in control, and hearing them say that's right signals they truly feel understood.
Open questions that start with how or what give the other side the feeling of control while quietly steering them toward solving your problem.

lessons.t: Hunt for the Hidden Black Swans
lessons.b: Every tool in the book serves one purpose: uncovering the surprising unknown facts that can transform a deal, instead of settling for splitting the difference.

books.blurb: Chris Voss spent years as the FBI's lead international kidnapping negotiator. In this book he argues that most negotiation advice gets people wrong. We are not calm, rational deal makers. We are emotional creatures who decide with our feelings first. So the best negotiators don't argue harder. They listen better. Voss calls this tactical empathy: understanding the other side's feelings and showing them you understand. He turns it into practical tools you can use anywhere, from salary talks to buying a car to getting your kids to bed. These tools include repeating someone's last words back to them, naming their emotions out loud, inviting them to say no, and asking open questions that start with how or what. The goal is never a lazy compromise. It is uncovering hidden information that changes everything.

books.title: The 4 Disciplines of Execution
books.author: Chris McChesney, Sean Covey, and Jim Huling

lessons.b: The biggest threat to any important goal is the whirlwind, the urgent daily work that consumes the time and energy needed for anything new.

lessons.t: The Four Disciplines at a Glance
lessons.b: Execution becomes reliable when teams practise four connected disciplines: focus, lead measures, a scoreboard, and regular accountability.
Discipline 1 says the more goals you chase at once, the fewer you achieve, so pick one or two that truly matter most.

lessons.t: From X to Y by When
lessons.b: A wildly important goal must be measurable and time-bound, written as moving from a starting line to a finish line by a deadline.
Discipline 2 says to track the predictive actions you can influence, like daily calories and exercise, rather than only the end result, like weight lost.
Discipline 3 says a simple, visible scoreboard showing whether the team is winning drives far more engagement than a complex report.
Discipline 4 says short, regular team sessions, where people report on last week's commitments and make new ones, keep the goal alive.
The four disciplines work together to protect a small slice of time for your top goal, so progress happens even while the whirlwind keeps blowing.

books.blurb: Most leaders can set a strategy. Far fewer can get it done. This book argues that the real enemy of execution is not laziness or bad ideas but the whirlwind, the endless urgent work that keeps the day running and swallows everything new. To break through, the authors offer four disciplines. First, focus on one or two wildly important goals instead of many. Second, act on lead measures, the small actions you control that drive results, rather than obsessing over lagging outcomes. Third, keep a simple, compelling scoreboard so the team always knows whether it is winning. Fourth, create a cadence of accountability through short weekly meetings where everyone commits to specific actions. Together, these disciplines turn vague strategy into steady, visible progress, even while the whirlwind keeps blowing.

books.title: 10x Rule
books.author: Grant Cardone
books.blurb: Grant Cardone argues that most people fail not because they lack talent, but because they badly underestimate what success will take. His fix is the 10X Rule. Set targets ten times bigger than you think you need, then take ten times the action you think is required. Along the way, he sorts behavior into four degrees of action: doing nothing, retreating, normal action, and massive action. Only massive action reliably gets results. Cardone treats success as a duty rather than a luxury, and warns that aiming for average is a quiet way to fail. He urges readers to stop competing and start dominating their field, and to read fear and criticism as signs of progress. The book's tone is relentless and motivational. Its central message is simple: think bigger, do far more, and never stop expanding.

lessons.t: Why Everyone Underestimates What Success Takes
lessons.b: Most goals fail because people miscalculate the time, effort, and energy required, so they plan for far too little.
Aim ten times higher than feels reasonable, because big targets demand new thinking and even missing them leaves you far ahead.
You can take no action, retreat, take normal action, or take massive action, and only massive action consistently creates success.
Doing what most people do yields average results, and average leaves you exposed when life gets hard.
Instead of chasing competitors, do so much more that you own your market and others end up chasing you.
When you see success as an obligation and read fear and criticism as signs of progress, massive action becomes a way of life.

books.title: Mindset
books.author: Carol S. Dweck
books.blurb: Psychologist Carol Dweck argues that people hold one of two broad beliefs about their abilities. In a fixed mindset, talent and intelligence are set traits, so every challenge becomes a test of worth and failure feels like a verdict. In a growth mindset, abilities can be developed through effort, good strategies and help from others, so challenges become chances to learn. Drawing on decades of research and examples from school, sports, business and relationships, Dweck shows how these mindsets shape whether people seek challenges, persist through setbacks, accept feedback and celebrate others' success. She explains how praise, parenting, teaching and leadership can push people toward one mindset or the other. Most importantly, she argues that mindsets themselves can change, and offers practical ways to notice your fixed-mindset voice and choose growth instead.

lessons.b: Whether you believe ability is fixed or can grow changes how you interpret almost every challenge you face.

lessons.t: Failure as Verdict or as Information
lessons.b: A fixed mindset treats setbacks and effort as proof of inadequacy, while a growth mindset treats them as the path to improvement.
Even celebrated stars in sports and other fields became great through practice and learning, not talent alone.

lessons.t: Praise the Process, Not the Person
lessons.b: Praising intelligence makes people avoid challenges, while praising effort and strategy makes them seek challenges and persist.

lessons.t: Leaders Who Learn Versus Leaders Who Prove
lessons.b: Fixed-mindset leaders need to look superior and silence bad news, while growth-mindset leaders build teams that learn and adapt.
Believing good relationships should be effortless makes problems feel fatal, while a growth mindset sees conflict as something partners can work through.
You can shift toward growth by noticing your fixed-mindset voice, answering it, and treating every skill as not yet mastered rather than impossible.
